One Nation's Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce travelled to Melbourne for a fundraising event today. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

Pauline Hanson has denied a One Nation fundraising event in Melbourne was relocated because of protesters.

Senator Hanson and MP Barnaby Joyce were both slated to speak at the fundraiser as of Friday evening, which was meant to be held at Giorgio Casa, an Italian restaurant in Moonee Ponds in Melbourne's inner-north.

A spokesperson for the party initially told the ABC the decision to move the event was prompted by advice from Victoria Police and the Australian Federal Police after concerns were raised about several protest groups vowing to demonstrate outside.

But speaking to reporters outside the event, Senator Hanson said the venue was changed because of "too many bookings".

"Do you think I'd be deterred by the protesters? Think twice. No. We just had so many people who wanted to come," she said.

About 20 protesters gathered around the venue in South Melbourne to rally against One Nation. (ABC News: Samantha Jonscher)

About 30 protesters attended the new location, shouting multiple slogans including, "Immigrants are welcome here, Nazis are not".

Mr Joyce said One Nation politicians and followers were not Nazis but supported the protesters' right to free political communication, as long as it did not become aggressive or threatening.

Dozens of police officers guarded the venue. Senator Hanson said it was a shame that was necessary, but she was excited to be in Melbourne.

Dozens of police officers surrounded the fundraising event in South Melbourne. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

"We are a democracy, and we actually have the right to have our say, have our opinion and put forward policies," she said.

Recent polling has shown a surge in One Nation's popularity across Australia, and Senator Hanson told reporters the party's "biggest membership [was] coming out of Victoria", which will have a state election in November.

One man was moved on by police outside the event.

"A 22-year-old man was given a direction to move on," a Victoria Police spokesperson said in a statement.

"As a matter of course, police will review any vision or CCTV from the evening."

The spokesperson said there were no arrests.

A Victoria Police spokesperson said it was not aware of any threats made to the original venue or event, but said it was the restaurant that decided to cancel the gathering.

"Police will maintain a presence in the area due to potential protest activity," the spokesperson said.

Several anti-racism groups had posted online rallying people to protest at the event, saying they planned to meet nearby, before marching to the restaurant.

Omar Hassan, a spokesperson for one of the groups organising tonight's demonstration, the Victorian Socialists and Campaign Against Racism and Fascism, said the group wanted to express that One Nation was "not welcome in Melbourne".

"The fight against One Nation and everything they stand for will continue," he said after news of the venue change emerged.

According to polling, One Nation is on track to win a swathe of seats in the November election. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

Speaking on 3AW, Mr Joyce said it was "disgraceful" that political discussion was being stifled in Victoria.

"If Carlton supporters can walk around with Collingwood supporters and both go to a pub and have a talk to Essendon supporters, then why can't we have a political event in Melbourne?" he said.

"Unless what you want is some sort of unilateral power structure of socialism that you're never allowed to question."

The Moonee Valley City Council had posted on social media earlier on Friday, warning the public to avoid the area during the protest if possible.

It comes just days after hundreds of people protested outside a One Nation event in Perth, which was met by a small group of counter-protesters.

Riding high in the opinion polls, which suggest One Nation is now the most popular political party in the country, Senator Hanson is travelling coast-to-coast, holding campaign-style fundraisers and meeting supporters.

Her online anti-Labor donation drive, "Fire the Liar", has raked in more than $3 million in less than three days, tripling the party's original $1 million target.

According to the website, about 50,500 Australians had contributed at last count. Donations averaged at about $60 per person.

On Thursday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese cast doubt on the legitimacy of the fundraiser, prompting One Nation to release an audit of the website by contractor and software engineer Daryl Monnink.

"Here's the independent audit that's just been completed that proves the site and money are ridgy didge," the post read.

"Now will the PM reveal how much his campaign has raised?"

The campaign went live on Wednesday morning in retaliation against Labor's latest donation drive, urging supporters to chip in and "Fund the Fight" against One Nation.
